name: Iwaidja
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Iwaidja (iwai1244) is not in the catalog. Both sweep-list titles are by Barbara Sayers. (1) Sayers & Pym 1977 'Notes on rhythmic patterning in Iwaidja' was found as an open PDF on the AuSIL publications page (https://ausil.org.au/language-documentation/ ->), saved and scanned, and read in full: it is a discourse-rhythm study and explicitly says word stress could not be identified by pitch; it gives no placement rule (prosody-but-not-word-stress; no catalog record). (2) Sayers 1977 'Prosodies in some Aboriginal languages' (WPNGL 20:91-100, Iwaidja + Wik-Mungkan per Glottolog) has no open copy anywhere reachable (archive.org holds only bibliography entries; sil.org search is JS/403; HathiTrust and Google Books blocked) — library-print-only, medium priority. The same AuSIL page also yielded the full PDF of Pym 1979 'An analysis of discourse phonology' (WP-A-2), the deciding source the earlier audit422 ladder flagged as unfetchable and the prior sweep had only as FTS snippets; its §2.1.6 (pp. 18-19) and p. 21 summary give the best first-hand Iwaidja word-stress statement: initial stress on the (max. 3-syllable) phonological word, shifting to the second syllable when that syllable begins a grammatical word, prefix an- always stressed, phrase/clause stress may override. The complete Pym & Larrimore 1979 phonemes paper was also fetched sources (silent on stress). All files, page pins, scanned text, search receipts and a dated addendum are under ( updated). all discovery went through archive.org APIs, Glottolog, ERIC API, AuSIL and curl.

new_statements.quote: 2.1.6 LEVEL 6 - THE PHONOLOGICAL WORD. Phonological words contain syllables which are grouped together rhythmically and carry at least a third degree of stress. Phrase or clause stress may also occur on the same syllable obscurring the word stress. Words are of three types: type 1: single syllable […] type 2: two syllables with stress on the first syllable 'ani- AB1, C2; -'pulan AB1, C5; type 3: three syllables with stress on the first syllable 'aritu- AB2, C4. [p. 18] On phonological words os [sic, = of] type 2 or 3 the stress will shift to the second syllable if that syllable marks the beginning of a grammatical word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the first syllable of the (phonological) word; where a phonological word of two or three syllables contains a grammatical-word boundary after its first syllable, stress moves to the second syllable, i.e. to the initial syllable of the grammatical word. Word stress is the lowest (third) degree in a hierarchy below phrase stress (second heaviest) and clause stress (heaviest), which can override it. Capell 1962 §1.7 (on file) independently states initial stress ('Stress is normally on the first syllable of a di- or trisyllabic word') and Shaw et al. 2020:584 restate initial primary stress for unprefixed nominals.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Pym 1979 (snippets seen) does not describe secondary word stress; it describes three degrees of stress at clause/phrase/word level. Capell 1962 §1.7: 'in four syllable words there is a secondary stress on the third syllable', with 'a trochaic rhythm built up based on initial stress' in longer words.
new_statements.exceptions: Pym 1979: stress shifts to the second syllable when it begins a grammatical word; 'The prefix an- always takes stress'; phrase or clause stress may obscure word stress; the study's stated aim was to find out 'why word stress appeared to vary'. Capell 1962: 'occasionally final stresses are found, as in /ga'ralg/, his body'. Evans 2009: in X-n-X total reduplicants either half may be more heavily stressed depending on higher-level prosody.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'phonological word' of a discourse-phonology hierarchy (levels: discourse > paragraph > sentence > clause > phrase/rhythm group > word > syllable), based on narrative and procedural texts recorded 1974, not citation forms; the greatest clause-level stress 'is normally in the verb'. Shaw et al. 2020's statement is restricted to unprefixed nominals (Iwaidja is a prefixing language).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Iwaidja proper (iwai1244; Capell 1962 calls it Jiwadja, Cobourg Peninsula). Shaw et al. 2020 and the Caudal/Mailhammer work are based on Croker Island (Minjilang) speakers, the surviving community; Pym's 1974 texts come from the same Croker Island community (speakers coded AB and RK). No dialect distinction is drawn in any stress statement.

new_statements.quote: Phonological words contain syllables which are grouped together rhythmically and carry at least a third degree of stress. Phrase or clause stress may also occur on the same syllable obscurring the word stress. Words are of three types: type 1: single syllable -'biñ; type 2: two syllables with stress on the first syllable 'ani-, -'pulan; type 3: three syllables with stress on the first syllable 'aritu-. [p. 19] On phonological words os [sic] type 2 or 3 the stress will shift to the second syllable if that syllable marks the beginning of a grammatical word. ... The prefix an- always takes stress.
new_statements.citation: Pym, Noreen. 1979. An analysis of discourse phonology. In Noreen Pym (with Bonnie Larrimore), Papers on Iwaidja phonology and grammar (Work Papers of SIL-AAB, Series A, vol. 2), 11ff. Darwin: SIL.
new_statements.locator: pp. 18-19, §2.1.6 'Level 6 - the phonological word'; summary p. 21 §2.2
new_statements.reading: Initial stress on the phonological word (max. three syllables: ['S], ['SS], ['SSS]), shifting to the second syllable when that syllable begins a grammatical word (i.e. when a phonological word straddles a grammatical-word boundary: [S'S], [S'SS]); the prefix an- is always stressed; phrase and clause stress (second-heaviest / heaviest) can sit on the same syllable and obscure word stress. Longer grammatical words are split into several rhythm groups, so the statement does not determine secondary-stress alternation in 4+-syllable grammatical words; Pym also states that syllable grouping matters more than stress placement, whose variation does not affect intelligibility. Agrees with Capell 1962 (initial primary, secondary on 3rd of 4) and Shaw et al. 2020 (initial for unprefixed nominals).

sources.citation: Sayers, Barbara J. & Noreen Pym. 1977. Notes on rhythmic patterning in Iwaidja. In Joyce Hudson (ed.), Five papers in Australian phonologies (Work Papers of SIL-AAB, Series A, vol. 1), 97-130. Darwin: SIL. [Glottolog 87018]
sources.quote: These notes are the result of two weeks' field work at Croker Island in September 1974 to seek a solution to stress, length and pitch problems. The problems in previous analysis had been in identifying word stress. This problem was due to looking for the highest pitch as the contrastive feature of word stress. However, in normal conversation (responses) and in words elicited in isolation the syllables with highest pitch fluctuated from utterance to utterance of the same word. Also within a word two or more syllables frequently appeared to be equally stressed--that is, they had the same pitch and intensity.
sources.locator: p. 97 §0 Introduction; also p. 98 §1, p. 99 §2, pp. 100-101 §3, p. 105 Texts legend
sources.note: Whole paper read (pp. 97-105 analysis + texts). It is a discourse-rhythm study (breath group > rhythm group > rhythmic segment, timing 'slow/fast' beats) and gives NO rule for where word stress falls. It reports that word stress could not be identified by pitch (pitch peaks fluctuate, syllables often equally stressed), that 'the high importance of timing and rhythmic segmentation in contrast to the relatively low importance of pitch' (p. 98) is the main finding, that 'main beat' rhythm groups 'could be called phonological words' and 'for the most part are equivalent to grammatical words' (p.…

Glottolog links the paper to Iwaidja and Wik-Mungkan; the title ('prosodies', Firthian sense) and Sayers' parallel Wik-Mungkan work ('Interpenetration of stress and pitch in Wik-Munkan', 1976) suggest a comparative treatment of stress/pitch/rhythm as prosodic features; the SIL 1985-86 catalog describes WPNGL 20 only as 'Includes articles on tagmemic theory, phonology, semantics,...'. Given that the companion Sayers & Pym 1977 paper found no identifiable word-stress rule, this 10-page comparative paper is unlikely to contain a placement rule not already in Pym 1979.
